claim: ATT&CK is the common language for attacker behaviour.
quote: We focus on ATT&CK-in-STIX because it is the most widely adopted public standard for representing adversary
issue: Ferraz says "most widely adopted public standard" (and "a widely adopted taxonomy", Sect. 1, PDF p. 1), about ATT&CK-in-STIX for cross-organisational CTI exchange. That is close to "common language" but not the same words, and Ferraz itself cites [22, 30] for it.

claim: CTI records which techniques an attack used, but rarely their order.
quote: In practice, however, CTI feeds rarely enumerate all steps, prerequisites, or action sequences. ... campaign and intrusion-set entries rarely encode temporal or causal information. Execution order, prerequisites, and environmental assumptions typically appear only in free text
locator: Sect. 2 (PDF p. 3); Sect. 1 (md copy, PDF p. 1)
issue: Ferraz is talking about structured CTI (STIX feeds, campaign and intrusion-set objects). It says the order "typically appear[s] only in free text", which means narrative reports do carry it. The dissertation's next sentence relies on exactly that (ChronoCTI recovers the order from report text). As written, "CTI ... rarely their order" covers reports too, and is wider than the source.
fix_text: "CTI records which techniques" -> "Structured CTI records which techniques"

claim: ATT&CK does not record the order of techniques either.
quote: Although ATT&CKin-STIX provides structured identifiers for techniques, tactics, campaigns, and intrusion sets, it does not directly encode temporal order, explicit prerequisites, environmental constraints, or branching logic.
issue: Ferraz measured ATT&CK v18.1, not v19.1. The structural point carries over.
